/-!
# Reducts of homogeneous structures (Thomas' conjecture)

"Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite relational language have finitely
many reducts?"

This is Thomas' conjecture (1991) on the reducts of countably infinite homogeneous structures in a
finite relational language. Here a *reduct* of a structure $M$ is a relational structure $N$ on
the same domain each of whose relations is first-order definable in $M$ without parameters, and
reducts are counted up to first-order interdefinability: two reducts are identified when each is
a reduct of the other, i.e. when they have the same relations definable without parameters.
(Counting reducts in the narrower sense of "forgetting some relation symbols" would make the
question trivial for a finite language.)

*Homogeneous* means ultrahomogeneous: every isomorphism between finite substructures of $M$
extends to an automorphism of $M$. Since such a structure is $\omega$-categorical, the conjecture
is equivalent to asking whether there are only finitely many closed permutation groups $G$ with
$\mathrm{Aut}(M) \le G \le \mathrm{Sym}(M)$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Reduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/reduct)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- S. Thomas, *Reducts of the random graph*, J. Symbolic Logic 56 (1991), 176–181.
  <https://doi.org/10.2307/2274912>
- M. Bodirsky, M. Pinsker, *Reducts of Ramsey structures*, Contemp. Math. 558 (2011), 489–519.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.6073>
-/
variable (L : FirstOrder.Language.{u, v}) (M : Type w) [L.Structure M]

blocks.code:
def definableRelations : Set (Σ n : ℕ, Set (Fin n → M)) :=
  {R | (∅ : Set M).Definable L R.2}
blocks.docstring:
The set of all finitary relations on `M` (recorded together with their arity) that are
first-order definable without parameters in the `L`-structure `M`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `Set.Definable` (used as the building block, with parameter set ∅) and `FirstOrder.Language.DefinableSet` (which is per fixed arity α and does not bundle all arities).
justification.name: Reduct.definableRelations
justification.why_needed: The set of all finitary relations on M (with arity) that are 0-definable in the L-structure M; this is the invariant that determines a structure up to first-order interdefinability. Needed to identify interdefinable reducts.

blocks.name: definableRelations

blocks.code:
def IsReduct {L' : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}} (N : L'.Structure M) : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (R : L'.Relations n), (∅ : Set M).Definable L {x | N.RelMap R x}
blocks.docstring:
A structure `N` on the same domain `M` (in a language `L'`) is a *reduct* of the
`L`-structure `M` if every relation of `N` is first-order definable without parameters in `M`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `FirstOrder.Language.LHom.reduct` — this is the purely syntactic reduct along a language map (omitting symbols), which would make the count trivially infinite/meaningless for the conjecture; `LHom.IsExpansionOn` is likewise syntactic.
justification.name: Reduct.IsReduct
justification.why_needed: Thomas' notion of reduct: a structure N (in language L') on the same domain M each of whose relations is first-order definable without parameters in M. Mathlib has no definability-based reduct notion.

blocks.name: IsReduct

blocks.docstring:
The reducts of the `L`-structure `M` up to first-order interdefinability. Each reduct `N`
(a structure on `M` in a relational language) is represented by the set of relations definable
without parameters in `N`; two reducts are interdefinable exactly when these sets coincide.

The reduct languages are taken in the universe of `M`. This loses nothing: every reduct is
interdefinable with the reduct whose relation symbols are its own relations, which are sets
of tuples of elements of `M`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: No Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib notion of interdefinability or of closed supergroups of Aut(M) in Sym(M) exists; the group-theoretic reformulation would additionally rely on the ω-categoricity theorem rather than the definition.
justification.name: Reduct.reductClasses
justification.why_needed: The set of interdefinability classes of reducts of M: each relational reduct N is represented by `definableRelations` of N, and two reducts are interdefinable iff these sets coincide, so `Set.Finite` of this set says 'finitely many reducts up to first-order interdefinability'.

blocks.name: reductClasses
blocks.text:
/-- The reducts of the `L`-structure `M` up to first-order interdefinability. Each reduct `N`
(a structure on `M` in a relational language) is represented by the set of relations definable
without parameters in `N`; two reducts are interdefinable exactly when these sets coincide.

The reduct languages are taken in the universe of `M`. This loses nothing: every reduct is
interdefinable with the reduct whose relation symbols are its own relations, which are sets
of tuples of elements of `M`. -/
def reductClasses : Set (Set (Σ n : ℕ, Set (Fin n → M))) :=
  {D | ∃ (L' : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) (_ : L'.IsRelational) (N : L'.Structure M),
    IsReduct L M N ∧ D = @definableRelations L' M N}

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 3]
theorem isReduct_self (L : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) [L.Structure M] :
    IsReduct L M ‹L.Structure M› := by
  intro n R
  refine ⟨(L.lhomWithConstants (∅ : Set M)).onFormula (Relations.formula R Term.var), ?_⟩
  ext x
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, LHom.realize_onFormula, Formula.realize_rel, Term.realize_var]
blocks.docstring: Every structure is a reduct of itself.
blocks.name: isReduct_self
blocks.text:
/-- Every structure is a reduct of itself. -/
@[category API, AMS 3]
theorem isReduct_self (L : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) [L.Structure M] :
    IsReduct L M ‹L.Structure M› := by
  intro n R
  refine ⟨(L.lhomWithConstants (∅ : Set M)).onFormula (Relations.formula R Term.var), ?_⟩
  ext x
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, LHom.realize_onFormula, Formula.realize_rel, Term.realize_var]

blocks.code:
@[category API, AMS 3]
theorem definableRelations_mem_reductClasses (L : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) [L.Structure M]
    [L.IsRelational] : definableRelations L M ∈ reductClasses L M :=
  ⟨L, inferInstance, ‹L.Structure M›, isReduct_self M L, rfl⟩
blocks.docstring: The interdefinability class of a relational structure is one of its own reduct classes.
blocks.name: definableRelations_mem_reductClasses
blocks.text:
/-- The interdefinability class of a relational structure is one of its own reduct classes. -/
@[category API, AMS 3]
theorem definableRelations_mem_reductClasses (L : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) [L.Structure M]
    [L.IsRelational] : definableRelations L M ∈ reductClasses L M :=
  ⟨L, inferInstance, ‹L.Structure M›, isReduct_self M L, rfl⟩

blocks.code:
@[category test, AMS 3]
theorem empty_mem_definableRelations (n : ℕ) :
    ⟨n, (∅ : Set (Fin n → M))⟩ ∈ definableRelations L M :=
  Set.definable_empty
blocks.docstring: The empty relation of every arity is definable without parameters in every structure.
blocks.name: empty_mem_definableRelations
blocks.text:
/-- The empty relation of every arity is definable without parameters in every structure. -/
@[category test, AMS 3]
theorem empty_mem_definableRelations (n : ℕ) :
    ⟨n, (∅ : Set (Fin n → M))⟩ ∈ definableRelations L M :=
  Set.definable_empty

blocks.code:
@[category research open, AMS 3]
theorem reduct : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (L : FirstOrder.Language.{u, v}) (M : Type w) [L.Structure M] [L.IsRelational]
      [Finite L.Symbols] [Countable M] [Infinite M],
      L.IsUltrahomogeneous M → (reductClasses L M).Finite := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Thomas' conjecture** (1991). "Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite
relational language have finitely many reducts?"

Precisely: is it true that for every countably infinite structure $M$ in a finite relational
language which is homogeneous (every isomorphism between finite substructures of $M$ extends to
an automorphism of $M$), there are only finitely many reducts of $M$ up to first-order
interdefinability? Here a reduct of $M$ is a structure on the domain of $M$ all of whose relations
are first-order definable without parameters in $M$. The conjectured answer is yes.
blocks.name: reduct
blocks.text:
/--
**Thomas' conjecture** (1991). "Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite
relational language have finitely many reducts?"

Precisely: is it true that for every countably infinite structure $M$ in a finite relational
language which is homogeneous (every isomorphism between finite substructures of $M$ extends to
an automorphism of $M$), there are only finitely many reducts of $M$ up to first-order
interdefinability? Here a reduct of $M$ is a structure on the domain of $M$ all of whose relations
are first-order definable without parameters in $M$. The conjectured answer is yes.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3]
theorem reduct : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (L : FirstOrder.Language.{u, v}) (M : Type w) [L.Structure M] [L.IsRelational]
      [Finite L.Symbols] [Countable M] [Infinite M],
      L.IsUltrahomogeneous M → (reductClasses L M).Finite := by
  sorry

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no question (Thomas' conjecture, 1991; conjectured answer 'yes', so answer(True) is the positive candidate): 'reducts' must be counted up to first-order interdefinability (structures on the same domain whose relations are definable without parameters in the original; for ω-categorical structures equivalently closed supergroups of Aut(M) in Sym(M)), otherwise the count is trivially infinite; 'finitely presented' is non-standard list-entry wording for the countable (countably infinite) ultrahomogeneous structures in a finite relational signature that the conjecture actually concerns, and the implicit quantifier is universal over all such structures.
claims.reviewer_why: c06 states the conjecture most literally: a reduct is a structure N on M in a relational language L' all of whose relations are ∅-definable (Mathlib `Set.Definable` with A = ∅) in M; interdefinability classes are represented by the set of ∅-definable finitary relations of N, so `(reductClasses L M).Finite` is exactly 'finitely many reducts up to first-order interdefinability'. Hypotheses `[L.IsRelational] [Finite L.Symbols] [Countable M] [Infinite M]` and Mathlib's `IsUltrahomogeneous` (= classical homogeneity for relational languages via `Substructure.fg_iff_finite`) match Thomas' conjecture; `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ ...` follows the repo style for questions, with answer(True) the positive answer. Edits: fixed the reduct-language universe to that of M (`Language.{w,w}`, which loses nothing since any reduct is interdefinable with the one whose symbols are its own relations) to remove free universe parameters from the theorem; adjusted API lemmas accordingly; added a small `test` lemma; expanded module docstring with references from c01/c02.
claims.source_text: Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite relational language have finitely many reducts?
claims.text_span: Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite relational language have finitely many reducts?

context: In universal algebra and in model theory, a reduct of an algebraic structure is obtained by omitting some of the operations and relations of that structure.  The opposite of "reduct" is "expansion".

decomposition_objections.text: None. The single slot and its notes (reducts up to first-order interdefinability, 'finitely presented' read as countable/countably infinite, universal quantification over all such structures, answer(True) as the positive candidate) match Thomas' 1991 conjecture and were followed.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Reducts of homogeneous structures (Thomas' conjecture)

"Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite relational language have finitely
many reducts?"

This is Thomas' conjecture (1991) on the reducts of countably infinite homogeneous structures in a
finite relational language. Here a *reduct* of a structure $M$ is a relational structure $N$ on
the same domain each of whose relations is first-order definable in $M$ without parameters, and
reducts are counted up to first-order interdefinability: two reducts are identified when each is
a reduct of the other, i.e. when they have the same relations definable without parameters.
(Counting reducts in the narrower sense of "forgetting some relation symbols" would make the
question trivial for a finite language.)

*Homogeneous* means ultrahomogeneous: every isomorphism between finite substructures of $M$
extends to an automorphism of $M$. Since such a structure is $\omega$-categorical, the conjecture
is equivalent to asking whether there are only finitely many closed permutation groups $G$ with
$\mathrm{Aut}(M) \le G \le \mathrm{Sym}(M)$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Reduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/reduct)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- S. Thomas, *Reducts of the random graph*, J. Symbolic Logic 56 (1991), 176–181.
  <https://doi.org/10.2307/2274912>
- M. Bodirsky, M. Pinsker, *Reducts of Ramsey structures*, Contemp. Math. 558 (2011), 489–519.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.6073>
-/

namespace Reduct

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language

universe u v w

variable (L : FirstOrder.Language.{u, v}) (M : Type w) [L.Structure M]

/-- The set of all finitary relations on `M` (recorded together with their arity) that are
first-order definable without parameters in the `L`-structure `M`. -/
def definableRelations : Set (Σ n : ℕ, Set (Fin n → M)) :=
  {R | (∅ : Set M).Definable L R.2}

/-- A structure `N` on the same domain `M` (in a language `L'`) is a *reduct* of the
`L`-structure `M` if every relation of `N` is first-order definable without parameters in `M`. -/
def IsReduct {L' : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}} (N : L'.Structure M) : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (R : L'.Relations n), (∅ : Set M).Definable L {x | N.RelMap R x}

/-- The reducts of the `L`-structure `M` up to first-order interdefinability. Each reduct `N`
(a structure on `M` in a relational language) is represented by the set of relations definable
without parameters in `N`; two reducts are interdefinable exactly when these sets coincide.

The reduct languages are taken in the universe of `M`. This loses nothing: every reduct is
interdefinable with the reduct whose relation symbols are its own relations, which are sets
of tuples of elements of `M`. -/
def reductClasses : Set (Set (Σ n : ℕ, Set (Fin n → M))) :=
  {D | ∃ (L' : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) (_ : L'.IsRelational) (N : L'.Structure M),
    IsReduct L M N ∧ D = @definableRelations L' M N}

/-- Every structure is a reduct of itself. -/
@[category API, AMS 3]
theorem isReduct_self (L : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) [L.Structure M] :
    IsReduct L M ‹L.Structure M› := by
  intro n R
  refine ⟨(L.lhomWithConstants (∅ : Set M)).onFormula (Relations.formula R Term.var), ?_⟩
  ext x
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, LHom.realize_onFormula, Formula.realize_rel, Term.realize_var]

/-- The interdefinability class of a relational structure is one of its own reduct classes. -/
@[category API, AMS 3]
theorem definableRelations_mem_reductClasses (L : FirstOrder.Language.{w, w}) [L.Structure M]
    [L.IsRelational] : definableRelations L M ∈ reductClasses L M :=
  ⟨L, inferInstance, ‹L.Structure M›, isReduct_self M L, rfl⟩

/-- The empty relation of every arity is definable without parameters in every structure. -/
@[category test, AMS 3]
theorem empty_mem_definableRelations (n : ℕ) :
    ⟨n, (∅ : Set (Fin n → M))⟩ ∈ definableRelations L M :=
  Set.definable_empty

/--
**Thomas' conjecture** (1991). "Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite
relational language have finitely many reducts?"

Precisely: is it true that for every countably infinite structure $M$ in a finite relational
language which is homogeneous (every isomorphism between finite substructures of $M$ extends to
an automorphism of $M$), there are only finitely many reducts of $M$ up to first-order
interdefinability? Here a reduct of $M$ is a structure on the domain of $M$ all of whose relations
are first-order definable without parameters in $M$. The conjectured answer is yes.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3]
theorem reduct : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (L : FirstOrder.Language.{u, v}) (M : Type w) [L.Structure M] [L.IsRelational]
      [Finite L.Symbols] [Countable M] [Infinite M],
      L.IsUltrahomogeneous M → (reductClasses L M).Finite := by
  sorry

end Reduct

items: 'Finitely presented' in the list entry is read (per the decomposition notes and Thomas' original conjecture) as 'countable'; formalized as `[Countable M] [Infinite M]` (countably infinite). Including `Infinite M` follows the notes' 'countably infinite'; the finite case is trivially true, so the statement is equivalent to Thomas' 'countable' wording either way.
'Finite relational language' is formalized as `[L.IsRelational] [Finite L.Symbols]` (no function symbols, including no constants; finitely many relation symbols in total).

'Homogeneous' is formalized with Mathlib's `FirstOrder.Language.IsUltrahomogeneous`: every embedding of a finitely generated substructure into M extends to an automorphism. For relational languages FG substructures are exactly the finite ones (`Substructure.fg_iff_finite`), and extending embeddings of finite substructures is equivalent to extending isomorphisms between finite substructures.

A reduct is taken in Thomas' sense: a structure N on the same domain M in a *relational* language whose relation symbols are all interpreted by sets first-order definable in M without parameters (`Set.Definable` with parameter set `∅`). Restricting reducts to relational languages matches the source; allowing function symbols with definable graphs would give the same interdefinability classes.

'Finitely many reducts' is counted up to first-order interdefinability: `reductClasses L M` is the set of `definableRelations` of reducts, so its finiteness is exactly finiteness of the number of interdefinability classes. The alternative reformulation via closed supergroups of Aut(M) in Sym(M) was not used since it relies on a theorem (Ryll-Nardzewski/ω-categoricity) rather than the definition.

The reduct languages range over `FirstOrder.Language.{u', v'}` with the theorem universe-polymorphic in u', v' (and in the universes of L and M). Every reduct in any universe is interdefinable with one in any fixed universe, so this is equivalent to the informal statement; universes are passed explicitly as `reductClasses.{u, v, w, u', v'}`.
Two `@[category API]` lemmas (`isReduct_self`, `definableRelations_mem_reductClasses`) were added as basic tests of the bespoke definitions, both with complete short proofs.
The theorem uses the `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ ...` yes/no form; `answer(True)` is the conjectured positive answer.

reviewer_notes: The list entry's 'finitely presented' is non-standard; following the decomposition notes and Thomas (1991) / Bodirsky–Pinsker it is read as countably infinite (Infinite M is harmless: finite structures trivially satisfy the conclusion). 'Reduct' is taken in Thomas' sense (∅-definable relations on the same domain, counted up to interdefinability), not the Wikipedia article's syntactic 'drop symbols' sense which would be trivially finite. All 8 candidates compiled and were faithful in content; differences were stylistic: c05/c07/c08 used answer(True) instead of the repo-preferred answer(sorry) for a question; c08 used the closed-supergroup (Ryll-Nardzewski) reformulation, equivalent but less literal; c04 fixed everything to universe 0; c01/c02/c03/c07 represented reducts via sets of relations and a bespoke 'relations-as-symbols' language (also faithful). c06 chosen as base for literalness and clean API lemmas.
statement: Does a finitely presented homogeneous structure for a finite relational language have finitely many reducts?
